1:4.t: "Did not have relations with her": the KJV's "knew her not", meaning sexual relations (see Genesis 4:1).

1:9.t: "The king's officials": the KJV's "the king's servants", meaning his court.

1:11.t: Bathsheba: the KJV spells it Bath-sheba.

1:21.t: "Lies down with his fathers in death": the KJV's "sleep with his fathers", the usual phrase for a king's death in Kings.

1:25.t: "Long live King Solomon": the KJV's "God save king Solomon". The Hebrew is "May the king live."

1:34.t: "Long live King Solomon": the KJV's "God save king Solomon". The Hebrew is "May the king live."

1:39.t: "Long live King Solomon": the KJV's "God save king Solomon". The Hebrew is "May the king live."
"The tent": the KJV's "the tabernacle", here the tent David had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:17).

1:38.t: Cherethites and Pelethites: foreign soldiers who formed David's personal guard, probably from Crete and Philistia.

1:40.t: "Flutes": the KJV's "pipes". "The ground shook": the KJV's "the earth rent", split.

1:47.t: "Congratulate": the KJV's "bless", in the sense of wishing well.

1:50.t: "The horns of the altar": its corners were shaped like horns, and holding them was a plea for sanctuary. Exodus 21:14 denies that protection to a deliberate murderer, which is why Joab is killed there (2:28-34).

2:4.t: "Watch how they live": the KJV's "take heed to their way". "Faithfully": the KJV's "in truth".

2:5.t: "Belt around his waist": the KJV's "girdle that was about his loins".

2:22.t: Asking for a dead king's concubine was a claim to his throne (compare 2 Samuel 16:21-22), which is why Solomon reads Adonijah's request as a bid for the kingdom.

2:23.t: "May God deal with me severely, and more so": the KJV's "God do so to me, and more also", a standard oath formula.

2:24.t: "A royal house": the KJV's "an house", meaning a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:11).

2:25.t: "Struck him down": the KJV's "fell upon him", meaning attacked and killed.

2:29.t: "Struck him down": the KJV's "fell upon him", meaning attacked and killed.

2:46.t: "Struck him down": the KJV's "fell upon him", meaning attacked and killed.

2:28.t: "The tent of the LORD": the KJV's "tabernacle of the LORD", the tent David had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem, as at 1:39.

2:37.t: "The Kidron Valley": the KJV's "the brook Kidron", a stream bed east of Jerusalem, dry for much of the year.

2:39.t: Maacah: the KJV spells it Maachah. "Slaves": the KJV's "servants".

3:1.t: "Made an alliance by marriage": the KJV's "made affinity". "Palace": the KJV's "his own house".

3:7.t: "Go out or come in": a Hebrew way of saying how to lead and conduct affairs, especially in war.

3:9.t: "Govern": the KJV's "judge"; in Israel the king's main task was to judge, that is, to rule and settle disputes.

"Understanding heart" (Hebrew lev shomea, literally "a listening heart"): the heart in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will more than of feeling. Solomon asks for a mind that listens, to God and to those who come before him for judgment.

3:11.t: "Govern": the KJV's "judge"; in Israel the king's main task was to judge, that is, to rule and settle disputes.

3:10.t: "The Lord": the KJV prints "Lord" (not LORD) here, following the Hebrew Adonai.

3:14.t: "Give you a long life": the KJV's "lengthen thy days".

3:19.t: "She lay on him": the KJV's "she overlaid it".

3:26.t: "Her heart ached with love": the KJV's "her bowels yearned upon her son"; the Hebrew places tender feeling in the inner parts.

4:2.t: "Chief officials": the KJV's "princes". "Azariah the son of Zadok the priest" can mean that Azariah or Zadok was the priest.

4:3.t: Ahijah: the KJV spells it Ahiah. "Secretaries": the KJV's "scribes", royal secretaries.

4:5.t: "Chief officer": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word is kohen, normally "priest", and some modern Bibles read "a priest".

4:6.t: "Forced labor": the KJV's "tribute", here meaning labor gangs drafted for the king's work.

4:8.t: "The son of Hur" and the others: the KJV's wording is kept. In Hebrew these are names, Ben-hur, Ben-deker and so on.

4:10.t: Arubboth, Socoh, Zarethan: the KJV spells them Aruboth, Sochoh, Zartanah.

4:12.t: Arubboth, Socoh, Zarethan: the KJV spells them Aruboth, Sochoh, Zartanah.

4:13.t: "Sixty": the KJV's "threescore". "Bronze": the KJV's "brasen"; "brass" in 1611 meant copper or bronze (see Genesis 4:22).

4:15.t: Basemath: the KJV spells it Basmath.

4:21.t: "The Euphrates", "the River": the KJV's "the river". "West of the Euphrates": the KJV's "on this side the river", seen from Israel.

4:24.t: "The Euphrates", "the River": the KJV's "the river". "West of the Euphrates": the KJV's "on this side the river", seen from Israel.
Gaza: the KJV spells it Azzah here.

4:22.t: KJV: "thirty measures of fine flour, and threescore measures of meal". The measure here is the cor (about 220 liters).

4:23.t: "Deer, gazelles, roebucks": the KJV's "harts, and roebucks, and fallowdeer"; the exact animals are uncertain.

4:26.t: KJV: "forty thousand stalls of horses ... twelve thousand horsemen". The parallel in 2 Chronicles 9:25 has 4,000 stalls; the difference is probably a copying error.

4:28.t: "Swift steeds": the KJV's "dromedaries"; the Hebrew means fast horses.

4:29.t: "Breadth of mind": the KJV's "largeness of heart".

4:30.t: "The people of the east": the KJV's "the children of the east country", the peoples of the desert east of Israel, known for wisdom.

4:31.t: Calcol: the KJV spells it Chalcol.

4:32.t: KJV: "three thousand proverbs ... a thousand and five".

5:1.t: "A friend of": the KJV's "a lover of", meaning an ally on good terms.

5:4.t: "Misfortune": the KJV's "evil occurrent", an old word for something that happens.

5:6.t: Sidonians: the KJV spells it Zidonians in some places; the people of Sidon, a Phoenician city north of Tyre.

5:8.t: "Cypress": the KJV's "fir". The Hebrew berosh is a tall conifer, probably cypress or juniper.

5:10.t: "Cypress": the KJV's "fir". The Hebrew berosh is a tall conifer, probably cypress or juniper.

5:11.t: KJV: "twenty thousand measures of wheat ... and twenty measures of pure oil", measured in cors. "Pressed olive oil": the KJV's "pure oil", oil from beaten olives, the finest grade.

5:14.t: KJV: "thirty thousand", "ten thousand", "threescore and ten thousand", "fourscore thousand", "three thousand and three hundred". 2 Chronicles 2:18 gives 3,600 overseers.

5:18.t: "The men of Gebal": the KJV's "the stonesquarers". The Hebrew is the name of the Phoenician city Gebal (Byblos), whose people were known as builders.

6:1.t: KJV: "the four hundred and eightieth year". Ziv: the KJV spells it Zif; the second month, in April and May.

6:2.t: KJV: threescore cubits long, twenty wide, thirty high.

6:3.t: "Main hall": the KJV's "temple", here meaning the large outer room of the house, as distinct from the inner sanctuary. KJV: porch twenty cubits by ten.

6:4.t: "Windows with narrow frames": the KJV's "windows of narrow lights". The Hebrew may mean windows with recessed frames or latticed windows.

6:5.t: "Inner sanctuary": the KJV's "oracle", the innermost room, also called the Most Holy Place (6:16).

6:6.t: KJV: five, six and seven cubits. "Offset ledges": the KJV's "narrowed rests", steps in the outer wall on which the beams of each story rested.

6:7.t: "Finished at the quarry": the KJV's "made ready before it was brought thither".

6:8.t: "The south side": the KJV's "the right side", facing east, which is south. "Middle story" follows the KJV; the Greek Old Testament reads "lowest".

6:15.t: "Rafters of the ceiling": the KJV's "walls of the cieling".

6:16.t: KJV: "twenty cubits". The Most Holy Place: the KJV's "the most holy place".

6:18.t: "Gourds": the KJV's "knops", round ornaments shaped like gourds.

6:20.t: KJV: twenty cubits each way; cherubim ten cubits high, each wing five cubits.
"The altar of cedar": the incense altar in front of the inner sanctuary.

6:23.t: KJV: twenty cubits each way; cherubim ten cubits high, each wing five cubits.
Cherubim: the KJV's "cherubims"; cherubim is already the Hebrew plural. "Olive wood": the KJV's "olive tree"; the Hebrew may mean wild olive or pine.

6:31.t: "Took up a fifth of the wall", "a fourth of the wall": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew is unclear, and many modern Bibles read "five-sided" and "four-sided" doorframes.

6:33.t: "Took up a fifth of the wall", "a fourth of the wall": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew is unclear, and many modern Bibles read "five-sided" and "four-sided" doorframes.

6:38.t: Bul: the eighth month, in October and November.

7:2.t: KJV: "an hundred cubits ... fifty cubits ... thirty cubits". The House of the Forest of Lebanon was named for its many cedar pillars.

7:4.t: "Window facing window": the KJV's "light was against light".

7:6.t: KJV: "fifty cubits ... thirty cubits". "Hall of Pillars": the KJV's "porch of pillars"; the same Hebrew word is used for the halls in verses 6-8. "Canopy": the KJV's "thick beam"; the Hebrew is uncertain.

7:7.t: "From floor to floor": as in the KJV; the Hebrew may mean from floor to rafters.

7:8.t: "Behind the hall": the KJV's "within the porch".

7:9.t: "The top of the walls": the KJV's "the coping".

7:10.t: KJV: "stones of ten cubits, and stones of eight cubits".

7:13.t: This Hiram is a craftsman, not King Hiram of 5:1. 2 Chronicles 2:14 calls his mother a woman of Dan; she may have been of Danite descent living in Naphtali.

7:14.t: "Bronze": the KJV's "brass", which in 1611 meant copper or bronze (see Genesis 4:22).

7:15.t: KJV: "eighteen cubits high apiece: and a line of twelve cubits did compass either of them".

7:16.t: "Capitals": the KJV's "chapiters", the decorated tops of the pillars. KJV: five cubits high (7:16), four cubits (7:19).

7:18.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult; the KJV's sense is followed.

7:20.t: "Rounded part": the KJV's "belly". "On each capital": the KJV's "upon the other chapiter".

7:21.t: Jachin probably means "He establishes"; Boaz probably means "in Him is strength".

7:23.t: "The Sea of cast metal": the KJV's "a molten sea", a huge bronze basin for the priests' washing (2 Chronicles 4:6). KJV: ten cubits across, five high, a line of thirty cubits around.

7:24.t: "Gourds": the KJV's "knops", round ornaments shaped like gourds, as at 6:18. KJV: "ten in a cubit".

7:26.t: KJV: "an hand breadth thick ... it contained two thousand baths". 2 Chronicles 4:5 has 3,000 baths.

7:27.t: KJV: four cubits by four by three. "Stands": the KJV's "bases", wheeled carts for the basins.

7:28.t: The construction of the stands is hard to follow in the Hebrew. "Panels" and "frames" are the KJV's "borders" and "ledges"; "supports" are its "undersetters"; "wreaths" are its "additions"; "rims" and "hubs" are its "felloes" and "naves".

7:31.t: KJV: "a cubit ... a cubit and an half". 7:32 KJV: "a cubit and half a cubit". 7:35 KJV: "half a cubit high".

7:38.t: KJV: "one laver contained forty baths: and every laver was four cubits". "Basins": the KJV's "lavers".

7:39.t: "South side", "north side": the KJV's "right side" and "left side", facing east. "At the southeast corner": the KJV's "eastward over against the south".

7:50.t: "Wick trimmers": the KJV's "snuffers". "Dishes": the KJV's "spoons", small dishes for incense. "Firepans": the KJV's "censers". "Sockets": the KJV's "hinges".

7:46.t: Zarethan: the KJV spells it Zarthan here.

7:48.t: "The bread of the Presence": the KJV's "shewbread", the twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath.

7:49.t: "Lampstands": the KJV's "candlesticks"; they held oil lamps, not candles.

8:2.t: Ethanim: the seventh month, in September and October. The feast is the Feast of Shelters (Tabernacles).

8:4.t: "The tent of meeting": the KJV's "the tabernacle of the congregation", the tent made under Moses.

8:8.t: "Drew the poles out so far": the KJV's "drew out the staves". The Hebrew may mean the poles were long.

8:9.t: "Tablets": the KJV's "tables", the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments.

8:23.t: "Showing kindness": the KJV's "mercy", the Hebrew hesed, loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant (see Genesis 24:27).

"Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it (see Genesis 24:27). God's hesed is rendered "steadfast love"; a person's hesed is "kindness" (2:7). At 20:31 the KJV's "merciful kings" is the related adjective, kings known for keeping faith and showing mercy. At 3:6 "faithfulness" is emet, firmness and reliability, which the KJV renders "truth".

8:25.t: "Watch how they live": the KJV's "take heed to their way", as at 2:4.

8:27.t: "The highest heaven": the KJV's "heaven of heavens".

8:32.t: "Declare the innocent in the right": the KJV's "justifying the righteous", in the sense of a judge's verdict.

8:37.t: "Grasshoppers": the KJV's "caterpiller"; the Hebrew names a kind of locust.

8:47.t: "Come to their senses": the KJV's "bethink themselves".

"Repent", "return" (Hebrew shuv): the basic meaning is to turn around or come back. The same verb describes the people turning back to God in repentance and returning home from exile, and the prayer plays on both.

8:51.t: "Iron furnace": a smelting furnace, a picture of the hardship of Egypt.

8:61.t: "Wholly devoted": the KJV's "perfect", meaning whole and upright, as at Genesis 6:9.

8:63.t: KJV: "two and twenty thousand oxen, and an hundred and twenty thousand sheep".

8:64.t: "Grain offerings": the KJV's "meat offerings", in the old sense of food.

8:65.t: "Lebo-hamath": the KJV's "the entering in of Hamath", the northern limit of Israel. "The Brook of Egypt": the KJV's "the river of Egypt", a stream bed at the southwest border, not the Nile.

8:66.t: "Went to their homes": the KJV's "went unto their tents", an old phrase for going home.

9:8.t: "Which is now so exalted": the KJV's "which is high". Some modern Bibles read "will become a heap of ruins", following ancient translations.

9:13.t: Cabul sounds like the Hebrew for "as nothing", that is, worthless.

9:15.t: "The Millo": a terraced structure or fill, probably on the slope of the City of David; the name means "filling".

9:16.t: "Wedding gift": the KJV's "a present", a dowry.

9:21.t: "Slave laborers": the KJV's "a tribute of bondservice".

9:23.t: KJV: "five hundred and fifty". 2 Chronicles 8:10 has 250, counting a different group of overseers.

9:26.t: "Fleet": the KJV's "navy". Elath: the KJV spells it Eloth.

9:28.t: KJV: "four hundred and twenty talents". Ophir was a land known for gold, perhaps in southern Arabia or East Africa.

10:1.t: "Test": the KJV's "prove". Sheba was a kingdom in southern Arabia.

10:3.t: "Answered all her questions": the KJV's "told her all her questions".

10:5.t: "It took her breath away": the KJV's "there was no more spirit in her". "The stairway by which he went up": the KJV's "his ascent". The Hebrew can also mean "the burnt offerings he offered", as some modern Bibles read.

10:10.t: KJV: "an hundred and twenty talents of gold".

10:11.t: "Almug wood": a costly wood, perhaps red sandalwood; 2 Chronicles 9:10 spells it algum. "Supports": the KJV's "pillars"; the Hebrew word is uncertain and may mean railings or steps. "Lyres and harps": the KJV's "harps also and psalteries".

10:14.t: KJV: "six hundred threescore and six talents of gold".

10:16.t: KJV: "six hundred shekels of gold went to one target" and "three pound of gold went to one shield". "Large shields": the KJV's "targets", body-length shields. The pound here is the maneh (about 570 grams).

10:22.t: "Ships of Tarshish": the KJV's "a navy of Tharshish", large seagoing ships of the kind that sailed to Tarshish, probably in Spain. "Peacocks": as in the KJV; the Hebrew word may mean baboons.

10:27.t: "Sycamore-fig trees": the KJV's "sycomore trees", a kind of fig tree, not the North American sycamore. "Lowlands": the KJV's "the vale", the Shephelah, the foothills west of Judah.

10:28.t: "Linen yarn": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word is now generally read as the place name Kue (Cilicia, in southern Turkey), so that many modern Bibles read "from Egypt and Kue".

10:29.t: KJV: "six hundred shekels of silver, and an horse for an hundred and fifty". Aram: the KJV's "Syria"; the Arameans lived in what is now Syria.

11:1.t: "Foreign women": the KJV's "strange women", meaning women from other nations.

11:8.t: "Foreign women": the KJV's "strange women", meaning women from other nations.

11:2.t: "Intermarry with": the KJV's "go in to them".

11:3.t: KJV: "seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines". A concubine was a wife of lower rank.

11:4.t: "Wholly devoted": the KJV's "perfect", meaning whole and upright, as at 8:61.

11:5.t: Ashtoreth: a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war (Astarte). Milcom: the national god of Ammon, probably the same as Molech (11:7).
"Detestable god": the KJV's "abomination", a word used of idols as things God hates.

11:33.t: Ashtoreth: a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war (Astarte). Milcom: the national god of Ammon, probably the same as Molech (11:7).

11:7.t: "Detestable god": the KJV's "abomination", a word used of idols as things God hates.
"The hill east of Jerusalem": the KJV's "the hill that is before Jerusalem", the Mount of Olives.

11:14.t: "Adversary": the Hebrew is satan, used here in its ordinary sense of an opponent.

11:23.t: Eliada: the KJV spells it Eliadah.

11:26.t: Ephraimite: the KJV's "Ephrathite", which here means a man of Ephraim. Zeredah: the KJV spells it Zereda. "Rebelled against": the KJV's "lifted up his hand against".

11:27.t: "Closing up the gap": the KJV's "repaired the breaches".

11:28.t: "Capable man": the KJV's "mighty man of valour". "Forced labor": the KJV's "charge", the labor gangs drafted for the king's work (see 5:13-14). The house of Joseph is the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.

11:31.t: Ahijah tore the cloak into twelve pieces but gives Jeroboam ten and reserves one for David's line. Judah and Benjamin stayed with Rehoboam (12:21); "one tribe" probably means Judah, with Benjamin counted with it.

11:36.t: "Lamp": the KJV's "light", a picture of a living heir on the throne.

11:38.t: "A lasting dynasty": the KJV's "a sure house".

11:41.t: "The Book of the Acts of Solomon": a royal record now lost, like the chronicles of the kings cited throughout Kings.

12:2.t: The KJV's verse 2 is part of a sentence that ends in verse 3. 2 Chronicles 10:2 says Jeroboam "returned out of Egypt", and some read this verse the same way.

12:11.t: "Discipline": the KJV's "chastise". "Scorpions" probably means whips tipped with sharp metal, a figure of harsher punishment.

12:14.t: "Discipline": the KJV's "chastise". "Scorpions" probably means whips tipped with sharp metal, a figure of harsher punishment.

12:15.t: "This turn of events": the KJV's "the cause".

12:16.t: "What share do we have": the KJV's "What portion have we". "To your tents": a call to go home and break away.

12:18.t: Adoram: the same man as Adoniram (4:6). "Forced labor": the KJV's "tribute", here meaning labor gangs drafted for the king's work, as at 4:6.

12:21.t: KJV: "an hundred and fourscore thousand chosen men".

12:29.t: Bethel: the KJV spells it Beth-el.

12:31.t: "Shrines on the high places": the KJV's "an house of high places". "From among all the people": the KJV's "of the lowest of the people"; the Hebrew means from every class, not only the poorest.

13:2.t: Josiah: this prophecy is fulfilled in 2 Kings 23:15-20.

13:6.t: "Plead with the LORD": the KJV's "intreat now the face of the LORD". The KJV source text carries a stray marginal note in this verse, which is not translated.

13:22.t: "Body": the KJV's "carcase", which in 1611 was used of human bodies too.

13:24.t: "Body": the KJV's "carcase", which in 1611 was used of human bodies too.

13:32.t: Samaria: the city was not built until Omri's reign (16:24); the name is used here for the northern kingdom as the writer knew it.

13:33.t: "From among all the people": the KJV's "of the lowest of the people"; the Hebrew means from every class, not only the poorest, as at 12:31. "Ordained": the KJV's "consecrated", literally "filled his hand", the phrase for installing a priest.

14:3.t: "Cakes": the KJV's "cracknels", a kind of hard biscuit. "Jar": the KJV's "cruse".

14:4.t: "His eyes had grown dim": the KJV's "his eyes were set".

14:10.t: "Slave or free": the KJV's "him that is shut up and left", a fixed phrase that probably means everyone, whether bound or free. "Every male": the KJV's "him that pisseth against the wall", a blunt idiom for every male, used in threats against a whole family line; see the Original language note on 14:10.

"Every male" (Hebrew mashtin beqir, "one who urinates against a wall"): the KJV renders it literally, "him that pisseth against the wall". It is a blunt idiom for every male, used in threats against a whole family line (also 16:11, 21:21; 1 Samuel 25:22). We give the meaning in plain words, since the literal phrase would distract today's reader.

14:14.t: "And what then? Even now it has begun": the KJV's "but what? even now". The Hebrew is abrupt and hard to read.

14:15.t: "Beyond the Euphrates": the KJV's "beyond the river".

"Asherah poles" (Hebrew asherah, plural asherim): the KJV's "groves". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar. The KJV followed the Greek and Latin in reading "grove", but the Hebrew says they were made, set up, cut down and burned, so a wooden cult object is meant. Where the goddess herself is meant (15:13, 18:19), we write Asherah.

14:19.t: "The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel": a royal record now lost, not the biblical books of Chronicles.

14:23.t: "Sacred pillars": the KJV's "images", standing stones used in Canaanite worship.

"Asherah poles" (Hebrew asherah, plural asherim): the KJV's "groves". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar. The KJV followed the Greek and Latin in reading "grove", but the Hebrew says they were made, set up, cut down and burned, so a wooden cult object is meant. Where the goddess herself is meant (15:13, 18:19), we write Asherah.

14:25.t: Shishak: the Egyptian king Sheshonq I, whose own inscription lists this campaign, about 925 BC.

15:2.t: Maacah: the KJV spells it Maachah. Abishalom is another form of Absalom. In verse 10 Maacah is Asa's grandmother; Hebrew "mother" can mean any female ancestor, and as queen mother she kept her rank into his reign.

15:10.t: Maacah: the KJV spells it Maachah. Abishalom is another form of Absalom. In verse 10 Maacah is Asa's grandmother; Hebrew "mother" can mean any female ancestor, and as queen mother she kept her rank into his reign.

15:13.t: "Queen mother": the KJV's "queen". The king's mother held an official rank at court. "Disgusting image for Asherah": the KJV's "an idol in a grove". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, whose symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree (see 14:15).

15:18.t: Tabrimmon: the KJV spells it Tabrimon. Ben-hadad means "son of Hadad", the Aramean storm god; several kings of Damascus bore the name.

15:19.t: "Let there be a treaty": the KJV's "There is a league"; the Hebrew has no verb and can be read either way.

15:20.t: Abel-beth-maacah, Chinneroth: the KJV spells them Abel-beth-maachah and Cinneroth. Chinneroth is the region of the Sea of Galilee.

15:23.t: "A disease in his feet": some take this as a polite phrase for a more serious illness; 2 Chronicles 16:12 says it was severe.

16:3.t: "Sweep away": the KJV's "take away the posterity of".

16:7.t: "Because he struck down Jeroboam's house": the KJV's "because he killed him". Baasha carried out God's judgment (15:29), but did it for his own ambition.

16:9.t: "Who was in charge of the palace": the KJV's "steward of his house".

16:11.t: "A single male": the KJV's "one that pisseth against a wall", a blunt idiom for every male, used in threats against a whole family line (see 14:10).

16:18.t: "Citadel": the KJV's "palace", the fortified inner part of the royal house.

16:24.t: KJV: "two talents of silver". Samaria (Hebrew Shomron) sounds like Shemer's name.

16:31.t: Sidonians: the KJV's "Zidonians". Ethbaal was king of Tyre and Sidon.

Baal: the word means "lord", "master" or "owner", and in ordinary Hebrew it can mean a husband. As a name it is the Canaanite storm god, believed to send rain and fertility, worshiped under many local forms (Baal-zebub, Baal-peor). Jezebel brought the Baal of Tyre into Israel, which is why the contest of chapter 18 turns on who sends the rain.

16:33.t: "An Asherah pole": the KJV's "a grove". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar (see 14:15).

16:34.t: "At the cost of": the KJV's "in", meaning the sons died as the work began and ended. Joshua had laid this curse on anyone who rebuilt Jericho (Joshua 6:26).

17:1.t: "One of the settlers of Gilead": the KJV's "who was of the inhabitants of Gilead"; the Hebrew word can mean a settler or a man from the town of Tishbe in Gilead. "Whom I serve": the KJV's "before whom I stand", a phrase for a servant waiting on his master.
Elijah: the name means "my God is Yahweh", a fitting name for the prophet who confronts the worship of Baal.

17:3.t: "East of the Jordan": the KJV's "before Jordan"; the Hebrew can also mean facing the Jordan.

17:5.t: "East of the Jordan": the KJV's "before Jordan"; the Hebrew can also mean facing the Jordan.

17:9.t: Zarephath was a coastal town between Tyre and Sidon, in Jezebel's homeland.

17:18.t: "What do you have against me": the KJV's "What have I to do with thee", an idiom of protest.

17:19.t: "Upper room": the KJV's "loft" and "chamber", a room built on the flat roof.

17:23.t: "Upper room": the KJV's "loft" and "chamber", a room built on the flat roof.

18:3.t: Obadiah: the name means "servant of Yahweh". This is not the prophet who wrote the book of Obadiah.

18:5.t: "Stream beds": the KJV's "brooks", wadis that run only after rain.

18:15.t: "Whom I serve": the KJV's "before whom I stand", a phrase for a servant waiting on his master, as at 17:1.

"The LORD of hosts" (Hebrew YHWH tseva'ot): "hosts" means armies, both the armies of Israel and the heavenly powers, the angels and the stars. The title presents the LORD as commander of every force in heaven and earth.

18:18.t: "The Baals": the KJV's "Baalim", the Hebrew plural, meaning the local forms of Baal.

18:19.t: "Prophets of Asherah": the KJV's "prophets of the groves". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, worshiped at wooden poles or carved trees (see 14:15).

18:24.t: "Your god": the KJV's "your gods"; the Hebrew elohim can mean either, and the prophets call on Baal alone.

18:27.t: "Deep in thought, or he has stepped aside": the KJV's "talking, or he is pursuing". The second Hebrew word is rare and may be a mocking hint that Baal is relieving himself.

18:28.t: "Swords and spears": the KJV's "knives and lancets".

18:29.t: "Raved on": the KJV's "prophesied", here meaning frenzied ecstatic behavior.

18:32.t: KJV: "two measures of seed", two seahs, about fifteen liters; perhaps meaning the area that much seed would sow.

18:43.t: "Seven times Elijah said, 'Go back'": the KJV's "Go again seven times".

18:44.t: "Harness your chariot": the KJV's "Prepare thy chariot".

18:46.t: "Tucked his cloak into his belt": the KJV's "girded up his loins", gathering a long garment so as to run.

19:2.t: "May the gods deal with me severely, and more so": the oath formula of 2:23.

19:3.t: "He saw this": as in the KJV. Many Hebrew manuscripts can be read "he was afraid".

19:4.t: "Broom tree": the KJV's "juniper tree", a desert shrub that gives some shade.

19:6.t: "Baked on hot stones": the KJV's "baken on the coals".

19:8.t: Horeb: another name for Mount Sinai, where God gave the law to Moses.

19:13.t: "Cloak": the KJV's "mantle", the prophet's outer garment, as in 19:19 and 2 Kings 2:8-14.

19:20.t: "What have I done to you?": the KJV's wording. It may mean "Go on, I have not stopped you", or "Consider what I have just done to you".

19:21.t: "Using the oxen's yoke and plow for fuel": the KJV's "with the instruments of the oxen". By burning his tools, Elisha left farming for good.

20:1.t: Aram, Arameans: the KJV's "Syria" and "Syrians"; the Arameans lived in what is now Syria, as at 10:29.

20:11.t: "The one who puts on his armor should not boast like the one who takes it off": the KJV's "him that girdeth on his harness", where harness means armor. Boast after the battle, not before it.

20:12.t: "Tents": the KJV's "pavilions", here temporary shelters in the field.

20:16.t: "Tents": the KJV's "pavilions", here temporary shelters in the field.

20:14.t: "The young men who serve the district governors": the KJV's "the young men of the princes of the provinces".

20:22.t: "Next spring", "in the spring": the KJV's "at the return of the year", the season when kings went to war.

20:26.t: "Next spring", "in the spring": the KJV's "at the return of the year", the season when kings went to war.

20:27.t: "Supplied": the KJV's "were all present"; the Hebrew means provisioned. "Goats": the KJV's "kids".

20:29.t: KJV: "an hundred thousand footmen", "twenty and seven thousand".

20:31.t: Sackcloth and ropes were signs of surrender and pleas for mercy.

20:34.t: "Market streets": the KJV's "streets", areas where merchants of one country traded in the other's capital.

20:35.t: "Companion": the KJV's "neighbour", here a fellow prophet.

"The sons of the prophets" (Hebrew bene ha-nevi'im): "sons of" in Hebrew often means members of a group or guild, not literal sons. These were communities of prophets, perhaps disciples gathered around a leading prophet such as Elijah or Elisha (2 Kings 2:3-15, 4:38, 6:1). "Sons of the prophets" is kept so that the reader can follow the phrase through Kings.

20:38.t: "Ashes over his eyes": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word can also mean a bandage or headband, as many modern Bibles read.

20:41.t: "Ashes over his eyes": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word can also mean a bandage or headband, as many modern Bibles read.

20:39.t: KJV: "a talent of silver", far more than a common soldier could pay.

20:43.t: "Sullen and angry": the KJV's "heavy and displeased".

21:3.t: Under the law, family land was not to be sold away for good (Leviticus 25:23), so Naboth refuses on principle.

21:10.t: "Cursed": the KJV's "blaspheme". The Hebrew literally says "blessed", a scribal way of avoiding writing "cursed God"; the sense is curse. 21:20-22 Elijah passes from his own words to the LORD's words without a break; the inner quotation marks follow that shift.

"Worthless men" (Hebrew bene beliya'al, "sons of Belial"): beliya'al probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing". The KJV keeps Belial as if it were a name, and by New Testament times it had become a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). In Kings it describes lawless, unscrupulous people, so we translate the sense.

21:13.t: "Cursed": the KJV's "blaspheme". The Hebrew literally says "blessed", a scribal way of avoiding writing "cursed God"; the sense is curse. 21:20-22 Elijah passes from his own words to the LORD's words without a break; the inner quotation marks follow that shift.

"Worthless men" (Hebrew bene beliya'al, "sons of Belial"): beliya'al probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing". The KJV keeps Belial as if it were a name, and by New Testament times it had become a name for Satan (2 Corinthians 6:15). In Kings it describes lawless, unscrupulous people, so we translate the sense.

21:21.t: "Every male, slave or free": the KJV's "him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel". The first phrase is a blunt idiom for every male; the second is a fixed phrase that probably means everyone, whether bound or free. See 14:10.

21:27.t: "Went about quietly": the KJV's "went softly", as a mourner.

22:6.t: "The Lord": the KJV prints "Lord" here, not LORD; the Hebrew is Adonai, a title that could fit any god, perhaps a hint that these prophets avoided the LORD's name.

22:10.t: "At the threshing floor": the KJV's "in a void place". The Hebrew means an open threshing floor, a flat area often used for public gatherings.

22:11.t: "Gore": the KJV's "push", as an ox with its horns.

22:23.t: "Pronounced disaster against you": the KJV's "spoken evil concerning thee".

22:27.t: "Scant rations of bread and water": the KJV's "bread of affliction and ... water of affliction". "Safely": the KJV's "in peace", here and in verse 28.

22:34.t: "At random": the KJV's "at a venture". "Between the joints of his armor": the KJV's "between the joints of the harness". "Turn around": the KJV's "Turn thine hand".

22:38.t: "They washed his armor": the KJV's reading. Most modern Bibles read the Hebrew as "and the prostitutes bathed".

22:39.t: "Ivory palace": the KJV's "ivory house", a palace decorated with ivory inlay; such ivories have been found at Samaria.

22:43.t: The Hebrew Bible splits this verse in two, so from here to the end of the chapter its verse numbers run one higher than the KJV's.

22:47.t: "A deputy ruled as king": Edom was then governed by an official under Judah.

22:48.t: "Tarshish": the KJV's "Tharshish", as at 10:22. "Ships of Tarshish" were large seagoing ships of the kind that sailed to Tarshish, probably in Spain.

2:6.t: "The grave" (Hebrew Sheol): the place of the dead, pictured as deep under the earth, where good and bad alike go. The KJV renders it "grave", "hell" or "pit". In the Old Testament it does not by itself mean a place of punishment. See Genesis 37:35.

2:9.t: "The grave" (Hebrew Sheol): the place of the dead, pictured as deep under the earth, where good and bad alike go. The KJV renders it "grave", "hell" or "pit". In the Old Testament it does not by itself mean a place of punishment. See Genesis 37:35.

3:2.t: "High places" (Hebrew bamot, singular bamah): open-air places of worship, often on hills, with an altar and sometimes a standing stone or Asherah pole. Some were used to worship the LORD, as at Gibeon, and some to worship other gods. Once the temple was built, Kings judges every king by whether he removed them, because Deuteronomy 12 calls for sacrifice only at the one place the LORD chooses. The KJV's "high places" is kept, since no other English phrase is clearer.

3:6.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it (see Genesis 24:27). God's hesed is rendered "steadfast love"; a person's hesed is "kindness" (2:7). At 20:31 the KJV's "merciful kings" is the related adjective, kings known for keeping faith and showing mercy. At 3:6 "faithfulness" is emet, firmness and reliability, which the KJV renders "truth".

3:15.t: "Peace offerings" (Hebrew shelamim): related to shalom, which means wholeness, well-being and being at peace with another, not only the absence of war. Part of the animal was burned, and the rest was eaten by the worshipers in a shared meal.

8:11.t: "The glory of the LORD" (Hebrew kavod): the root means weight or heaviness, and so honor and splendor. Used of God, it is His visible, overwhelming presence, often shown in the cloud, as when it filled the tabernacle at Exodus 40:34-35.

8:16.t: "My name will be there": in Hebrew thought a name stands for the person and his presence. The house is built "for the name of the LORD" because God, whom the heavens cannot contain (8:27), chooses to be present and to be called on there.

8:29.t: "My name will be there": in Hebrew thought a name stands for the person and his presence. The house is built "for the name of the LORD" because God, whom the heavens cannot contain (8:27), chooses to be present and to be called on there.

12:22.t: "Man of God" (Hebrew ish ha-elohim): a common title for a prophet in Kings, used of Shemaiah, the unnamed prophet of chapter 13, Elijah and Elisha. It means a man who belongs to God and speaks for Him, not a man who is divine.

12:28.t: "Here are your gods" (Hebrew elohim): the word is plural in form; it means God when used of the God of Israel, and gods when used of others, so the Hebrew here can mean "gods" or "God" (see Genesis 1:1). Jeroboam echoes Aaron's words over the golden calf (Exodus 32:4), and he may have meant the calves as pedestals for the LORD. Kings treats them as idols either way, and "the sin of Jeroboam" becomes the measure for every later king of Israel.

14:24.t: "Male shrine prostitutes" (Hebrew qadesh, literally "holy one" or "consecrated one"): the KJV's "sodomites". The word comes from the root for holiness and refers to men set apart for the service of a pagan shrine, where sexual rites were thought to be part of the worship. The KJV's word points to the conduct; our rendering keeps the link to the shrine.

16:13.t: "Worthless idols" (Hebrew hevel, plural havalim): the KJV's "vanities". hevel means breath or vapor, something that has no substance; it is the word behind "vanity of vanities" in Ecclesiastes. Applied to idols, it says they are empty and can do nothing.

16:26.t: "Worthless idols" (Hebrew hevel, plural havalim): the KJV's "vanities". hevel means breath or vapor, something that has no substance; it is the word behind "vanity of vanities" in Ecclesiastes. Applied to idols, it says they are empty and can do nothing.

17:21.t: "Life" (Hebrew nephesh): the KJV's "soul". Nephesh means a living, breathing creature, a whole person, not a soul separate from the body (see Genesis 2:7). Here it means the breath of life returning to the child's body, so "life" gives the sense better than "soul" does today.

18:21.t: "Waver", "leaped" (Hebrew pasach): the KJV's "halt" and "leaped". The verb means to limp or hobble. Elijah pictures the people limping between two paths, and the narrator uses the same verb for the prophets' ritual dance around Baal's altar, a sly echo the English cannot easily keep.

18:26.t: "Waver", "leaped" (Hebrew pasach): the KJV's "halt" and "leaped". The verb means to limp or hobble. Elijah pictures the people limping between two paths, and the narrator uses the same verb for the prophets' ritual dance around Baal's altar, a sly echo the English cannot easily keep.

19:7.t: "The angel of the LORD" (Hebrew malakh YHWH): malakh means messenger, human or heavenly. "The angel of the LORD" sometimes speaks as God Himself (Genesis 16:10-13, Exodus 3:2-6), and interpreters differ on whether he is a created angel or an appearance of God. We keep "angel", lowercase, as the KJV has it.

19:10.t: "Zealous" (Hebrew qanna): the KJV's "jealous". The word means burning devotion that will not share a loved one with a rival. Used of God (Exodus 20:5), it is His claim to Israel's whole loyalty; Elijah claims to share that passion.

19:14.t: "Zealous" (Hebrew qanna): the KJV's "jealous". The word means burning devotion that will not share a loved one with a rival. Used of God (Exodus 20:5), it is His claim to Israel's whole loyalty; Elijah claims to share that passion.

19:12.t: "A still, small voice" (Hebrew qol demamah daqqah): the KJV's phrase is kept, since it is plain English and very well known. qol means voice or sound; demamah means stillness or silence, as of a calm after a storm (Psalm 107:29); daqqah means thin, fine or fine-ground. Literally "a sound of thin silence", it may mean a soft whisper or an almost silent hush. The point is the contrast: God was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, the signs of His power at Sinai, but made Himself known to Elijah quietly.

20:42.t: "Devoted to destruction" (Hebrew herem): the KJV's "appointed to utter destruction". herem is something or someone given over entirely to God, so that it may not be kept for human use; in war it meant total destruction (Joshua 6:17-18). Ahab sinned by treating God's verdict on Ben-hadad as a political bargain.
